question: A RAG system retrieves document B (cosine similarity 0.97 with the query) over document C (cosine similarity 0.71, L2 distance 0.15 from query embedding). A teammate argues the system should use L2 distance instead because document C is 'closer.' Which explanation best clarifies why cosine similarity is the appropriate metric here and what L2 distance is actually measuring?

options.A: Cosine similarity measures directional alignment in embedding space independent of vector magnitude, making it the correct proxy for semantic relatedness; L2 distance conflates direction and magnitude, so document C's low L2 reflects similar embedding norm to the query, not semantic closeness
options.B: L2 distance is always incorrect for retrieval tasks because embedding spaces are not Euclidean; only cosine similarity is mathematically valid in high-dimensional vector spaces
options.C: Document B has higher cosine similarity because its chunk size was smaller, producing a denser, more focused embedding that happens to align better with query direction
options.D: The choice of metric does not matter because all modern embedding models normalize output vectors to unit norm, making cosine similarity and L2 distance produce identical rankings

correct_explanation: Cosine similarity measures cos(θ) between two vectors — it is purely directional, ignoring magnitude. In semantic embedding spaces, what matters is the direction a document's representation 'points': semantically similar content should point in similar directions regardless of embedding norm (which can vary with document length, vocabulary density, or model internals). L2 distance measures Euclidean separation, which is sensitive to both direction and magnitude. A document with similar direction but different magnitude (e.g., shorter document) can appear 'far' under L2 while being semantically equivalent. The teammate's argument confuses geometric proximity in Euclidean space with semantic similarity.

distractor_explanations.B: High-dimensional embedding spaces are Euclidean. L2 distance is mathematically valid in them. The issue is not mathematical validity but which geometric property (direction vs. magnitude+direction) best captures semantic relatedness for a given embedding model.
distractor_explanations.C: Chunk size affects the content encoded in the embedding, not the geometric relationship between embedding direction and cosine similarity score. Cosine similarity does not systematically favor smaller chunks.
distractor_explanations.D: Not all embedding models normalize outputs to unit norm. Models like OpenAI's text-embedding series do produce unit-normalized embeddings (making cosine and normalized L2 equivalent), but many others (e.g., BERT-based models) do not. Even when normalized, the teammate's reasoning — that L2 should be used — would still be wrong in the non-normalized case, which is common.

question: An LLM with a 128k-token context window consistently ignores information placed in the middle 60% of a long document while reliably using information from the beginning and end. Which Transformer mechanism most directly explains this failure, and why does scaling the context window not automatically fix it?

options.A: Attention weight distributions are softmax-normalized and shaped by positional encoding; training data biases toward recency and primacy cause the model to systematically under-weight mid-sequence positions, and a larger context window extends this bias rather than correcting it
options.B: The KV cache evicts middle-sequence token representations under memory pressure during generation, making them unavailable to the attention computation
options.C: Softmax in self-attention clips gradient signals from mid-sequence positions to zero during fine-tuning, so the model never learned to use them regardless of context length
options.D: Transformer positional encodings are only defined for the first and last 10% of sequence positions; tokens in the middle receive a default zero encoding that the model learned to ignore

correct_explanation: The 'lost in the middle' phenomenon is a training distribution artifact. Models trained primarily on documents where the salient information appears at the beginning (introductions, abstracts) or end (conclusions, summaries) develop attention patterns that systematically under-weight mid-sequence positions. Positional encoding schemes (RoPE, ALiBi, sinusoidal) shape the attention score geometry, but they do not counteract the distributional bias learned from training data. Extending the context window via rope-scaling or similar techniques does not retrain the model's attention distribution — it merely allows longer inputs to be processed under the same biased attention behavior.

distractor_explanations.B: KV cache eviction (as in sliding window attention) is an explicit architectural choice made in models like Longformer or Mistral — not a default behavior in standard Transformers. Standard KV cache retains all positions up to the context limit. The failure is in attention weight distribution, not cache management.
distractor_explanations.C: Softmax does not clip gradients to zero. Gradients flow through softmax for all positions during training. The issue is a distributional bias in what receives training signal — not a gradient clipping mechanism that blocks learning for specific positions.
distractor_explanations.D: Positional encodings (RoPE, sinusoidal, ALiBi) are defined for all sequence positions up to the trained context length. There is no architectural gap at middle positions. The problem is emergent from training dynamics, not from encoding boundaries.

question: In a 20-layer network using sigmoid activations, gradients for layers 1–3 are effectively zero by the end of backpropagation despite healthy gradients at layer 20. Which property of the chain rule, combined with sigmoid's derivative, mechanistically produces this outcome?

options.A: The chain rule multiplies local gradients across layers; sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so propagating through 17 intermediate layers yields a factor of at most 0.25^17 ≈ 6×10⁻¹¹ — exponential collapse caused by repeated multiplication of sub-unity values
options.B: Backpropagation applies a depth cutoff: gradients are not computed for layers beyond a fixed depth from the output, and layers 1–3 fall outside this boundary for a 20-layer network
options.C: The vanishing gradient problem is caused by cross-entropy loss clipping gradient magnitudes to zero for high-confidence correct predictions; switching to MSE loss resolves it
options.D: PyTorch's autograd engine automatically clips gradients to zero for layers deeper than 10 to prevent numerical underflow in the computational graph

correct_explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule: ∂L/∂w₁ = (∂L/∂a_n) × ∏ᵢ(∂aᵢ/∂aᵢ₋₁). Each factor ∂aᵢ/∂aᵢ₋₁ is the local gradient through layer i's activation. For sigmoid, σ'(x) = σ(x)(1−σ(x)) ≤ 0.25. Multiplying 17 such factors (for a 20-layer net with healthy gradients at the output): 0.25¹⁷ ≈ 6×10⁻¹¹. This is machine-precision zero for 32-bit floats. The multiplicative nature of the chain rule is the mechanism: depth linearly multiplies the number of sub-unity factors, causing exponential gradient decay. This is why ReLU activations (derivative exactly 1 for positive inputs), residual connections (additive gradient paths), and careful weight initialization are critical for deep networks.

distractor_explanations.B: There is no depth cutoff in backpropagation. The algorithm computes gradients for every node in the computational graph regardless of depth. The vanishing gradient is a numerical phenomenon arising from the chain rule, not an algorithmic limit on graph traversal.
distractor_explanations.C: Vanishing gradients are independent of loss function choice. The collapse originates in activation function derivatives across layers. Cross-entropy vs. MSE changes only the gradient at the output layer (the first term in the chain rule product), not the multiplicative decay through intermediate layers.
distractor_explanations.D: Gradient clipping is a user-configured technique applied to prevent exploding gradients (values too large). It is not automatic, not depth-triggered, and rescales gradients when their global norm exceeds a threshold — it does not set them to zero.

question: A model achieves 97% accuracy on the training set and 61% on the validation set. Which mechanism most directly explains the gap, and what does it reveal about what the model actually learned?

options.A: The model memorized input-label associations specific to training examples rather than learning the underlying mapping, so it cannot generalize to unseen distributions
options.B: The validation set was drawn from a harder distribution by chance, so the gap requires no corrective action
options.C: The model's hypothesis class is too simple to capture the true function, causing high error on both splits
options.D: The learning rate is too high, causing the optimizer to overshoot the minimum during training and produce unstable weights

correct_explanation: A 36-point accuracy gap between train and validation is the defining signature of overfitting: the model memorized training-specific patterns, including noise, rather than learning a generalizable function. This is precisely what the held-out validation set is designed to detect — divergence between memorized performance and true generalization to unseen data.

distractor_explanations.B: Attributing the gap to dataset difficulty ignores its systematic nature. A random difficulty difference would not consistently produce a gap of this magnitude and would not shrink under regularization.
distractor_explanations.C: Underfitting produces low accuracy on both splits simultaneously. High training accuracy rules out underfitting — the model has sufficient capacity but directs it toward memorization rather than generalization.
distractor_explanations.D: Learning rate affects convergence dynamics but does not explain the train/val gap directly. A high learning rate produces noisy training curves, not consistently high training accuracy with low validation accuracy.

question: You are designing an agentic loop that executes multi-step tasks: it reads files, writes database records, and calls external APIs. Explain why idempotency is a non-negotiable requirement for each step, and describe the specific failure mode that occurs when a step is not idempotent and the agent crashes mid-execution then resumes.

In a Transformer's self-attention layer, a specific token attends almost entirely to itself (attention weight ≈ 0.98) with near-zero weight on all other positions. What does this behavior reveal about the Q/K/V computation, and what is the practical consequence for that token's contextual representation?

options.A: The token's query vector is highly aligned with its own key vector and misaligned with all others; after softmax, the output is nearly identical to the token's own value projection — the layer produces almost no contextual mixing for this token
options.B: This pattern is impossible because softmax distributes attention weights uniformly to prevent any single position from monopolizing the attention computation
options.C: High self-attention weight is the semantically correct behavior for tokens representing named entities, because the model learns to anchor entity representations to themselves
options.D: The value vectors for all other positions are near-zero at this layer due to residual connection saturation, collapsing the weighted sum to the self-attended value

correct_explanation: Attention weight from position i to position j is proportional to exp(Q_i · K_j / √d_k). If Q_i and K_i are strongly aligned while all other Q_i · K_j products are small, softmax produces a near one-hot distribution over position i. The attended output is then approximately V_i — the token's own value projection — with negligible contribution from surrounding context. The layer effectively becomes an identity operation for this token: it carries no new information from other positions. Multi-head attention mitigates this by running multiple attention heads, each of which may attend to different positions even if one head collapses.

distractor_explanations.B: Softmax does not enforce uniform distribution. Given inputs [10, 0.1, 0.1, ...], softmax produces a near one-hot output. The function maps arbitrary logit vectors to valid probability distributions, which can be arbitrarily peaked.
distractor_explanations.C: Attention weights are not trained to encode POS tags or entity classes. They emerge from learned Q/K projections optimized for next-token prediction or masked language modeling. Interpreting specific attention patterns as semantically meaningful is a post-hoc analysis with contested validity.
distractor_explanations.D: Value vectors are learned parameters initialized randomly and updated throughout training; they are not zero and do not saturate due to residual connections in a way that would collapse to self-attended values. The output is determined by the weighted sum of all value projections, governed by attention weights.

question: Mini-batch SGD with batch size 32 reaches a lower validation loss than full-batch gradient descent trained for the same number of epochs on identical data and learning rate. Which mechanism best explains this outcome?

options.A: Gradient noise from small batches acts as implicit regularization: it prevents the optimizer from settling into sharp, narrow minima that memorize training data, favoring flatter regions that generalize better
options.B: Smaller batches compute more accurate gradient estimates because they avoid averaging out rare but informative examples that full-batch averaging suppresses
options.C: Full-batch gradient descent always converges to saddle points in high-dimensional loss landscapes, while mini-batch noise escapes them
options.D: Mini-batch SGD performs more parameter updates per epoch, and a higher update count always produces better generalization regardless of the loss landscape geometry

correct_explanation: Mini-batch gradient estimates are noisy — they are unbiased estimates of the true gradient but with high variance. This noise is not merely a computational compromise; it functions as implicit regularization. Noisy gradient directions prevent the optimizer from converging to sharp local minima (which tend to overfit, as small parameter perturbations cause large loss increases) and instead explore flatter basin regions. Flat minima generalize better because the loss surface is stable around them. Full-batch GD follows the exact gradient and can be trapped in sharp minima with low training loss but poor test performance.

distractor_explanations.B: Smaller batches produce noisier, less accurate gradient estimates — not more accurate. The variance of the stochastic gradient estimator is inversely proportional to batch size. The benefit of mini-batch SGD is the noise itself, not estimation quality.
distractor_explanations.C: Full-batch GD can converge to local minima, not necessarily saddle points. In high-dimensional spaces, saddle points are common but not the only convergence failure mode. Full-batch GD can escape saddle points when the Hessian has negative curvature — it simply lacks the stochastic perturbation that helps mini-batch escape.
distractor_explanations.D: More updates per epoch does not directly cause better generalization. The number of updates affects convergence speed; the geometry of the solution found determines generalization. A model can take many gradient steps and still converge to a sharp, overfit minimum.

question: A RAG system uses fixed-size 512-token chunks with no overlap. Users report that answers are consistently incomplete when the relevant explanation spans a topic boundary that falls at a chunk boundary. Which mechanistic explanation best describes this failure and why semantic chunking addresses it?

options.A: Fixed-size chunking splits text at arbitrary token boundaries regardless of semantic coherence; a concept straddling a boundary becomes two partial vectors neither of which strongly represents the complete idea, so similarity search retrieves an incomplete fragment or misses both chunks entirely
options.B: 512 tokens is below the minimum sequence length for dense embedding models to produce meaningful vector representations, causing all chunks to cluster near the origin in embedding space
options.C: No-overlap chunking causes the embedding model to assign near-zero similarity between adjacent chunks because their token sequences never co-occur in the model's training window
options.D: Semantic chunking uses chunks of 2048+ tokens, which captures complete concepts through brute-force coverage of surrounding context

correct_explanation: Fixed-size chunking is content-agnostic: it creates vectors that represent arbitrary token windows, not coherent semantic units. When a concept explanation straddles a chunk boundary, each half is embedded independently. The first half's vector represents the setup without the conclusion; the second half's vector represents the conclusion without its motivation. Similarity search may retrieve one half (incomplete), the other half (out of context), or neither (since the query may not match either partial representation). Semantic chunking preserves natural language boundaries — paragraphs, sections — so each retrievable atom corresponds to a complete idea, producing an embedding that fully represents the concept for retrieval.

distractor_explanations.B: 512 tokens is a commonly used and well-supported chunk size. Most embedding models (e.g., text-embedding-3-small, BGE) are trained on sequences up to 512 or 8192 tokens and produce high-quality embeddings for shorter inputs. The failure is boundary alignment, not chunk size magnitude.
distractor_explanations.C: Embedding models do not compute similarity based on token co-occurrence between adjacent chunks at inference time. Similarity is computed as dot products in the learned embedding space. Whether tokens appear in adjacent chunks does not affect this computation.
distractor_explanations.D: Semantic chunking is not defined by a minimum size. It splits on natural language boundaries that may produce chunks shorter than 512 tokens. The benefit is semantic coherence of the unit, not coverage through larger size.
